overview: Mysore was a major southern Indian power under Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan, then a reduced Wodeyar kingdom under British supremacy. This map’s 1783 to 1815 coverage crosses the conquest of 1799. Its broad outlines do not accurately show the resulting territorial partition, and neither endpoint marks the kingdom’s founding or final disappearance.

periods.title: Tipu’s expanding struggle
periods.summary: Tipu inherited power in 1782 and sought French support against the East India Company.

periods.title: Territorial loss and final war
periods.summary: The 1792 settlement took half his dominions; the capital fell in May 1799.

periods.title: Restored dynasty, reduced independence
periods.summary: Wodeyar rule continued within a princely state subordinate to British power.

sections.title: Power, diplomacy and a changing kingdom

items.text: Haidar Ali rose through military leadership and took effective control of Mysore; his son Tipu ruled directly after him. Persian served as the court’s official language. The kingdom’s objects therefore speak in several ways: through royal images, Persian inscriptions and the Arabic religious phrases used on coins.

Srirangapatna, often called Seringapatam in older English records, stood on an island in the Kaveri River. It combined a royal capital with a fortress. Monsoon rains, river crossings and mountain routes mattered to the armies approaching it, as much as the strength of its walls.

After the 1792 war, two of Tipu’s sons were handed to Cornwallis as guarantees that the peace terms would be fulfilled. Robert Home painted the meeting. These royal children were drawn directly into diplomacy: a treaty could place members of a ruler’s family in an enemy’s custody.

Three ambassadors from Mysore arrived in Paris in July 1788 carrying cotton robes and jewellery for the French royal couple. They sought a military alliance and French manufactured goods. Louis XVI welcomed commercial ties, but the embassy did not secure the formal military alliance Tipu wanted.

The final attack on Srirangapatna on 4 May 1799 involved British armies and troops supplied by Hyderabad’s Nizam. Tipu was killed and his independent regime ended. The subsequent Mysore princely state preserved a dynasty and local government, but under a fundamentally different balance of power.

In 1800, Buchanan described ragi being ground as needed in a handmill near Srirangapatna. Its flour became a thick cooked pudding and cakes fried in oil. Preparing a meal began with processing the grain, long before anyone could ask whether dinner was ready.

Buchanan found firewood expensive around Srirangapatna. Women collected cattle dung, shaped it into cakes, dried them on walls and carried baskets into town to sell. Their work supplied cooking fires and a daily market. His account records practical recycling alongside the hard labour of gathering and carrying.

A bridge across the Kaveri’s southern branch also carried an aqueduct into the town and island. Buchanan described granite supports, stone beams and a channel lined with brick and plaster beside the roadway. The same structure helped people cross the river and brought water across it.

A portrait painted by Thomas Hickey around 1805 has been interpreted as showing Mysore royal women supporting smallpox vaccination. One woman presents her left upper arm. Historian Nigel Chancellor linked this gesture and the women’s jewellery with court encouragement of vaccination. The sitters’ identities and the picture’s purpose remain interpretations, rather than facts supplied by a caption on the canvas.

Mysore’s rockets used hammered iron casings attached to long bamboo poles or blades. The iron contained greater pressure than the paper-based casings common in contemporary European rockets. Metalworkers and military specialists helped develop a weapon that made a powerful impression on opposing armies.

Reports and captured rocket cases from India helped stimulate William Congreve’s experiments in Britain in the early nineteenth century. Mysore’s military defeat did not end its technical influence. A technology could travel into the workshops of a former opponent and be developed further there.

Tipu’s famous wooden tiger contains a small organ. Turning a handle made sounds and moved the arm of the European soldier represented beneath the animal. This elaborate palace object expressed hostility toward an enemy. Its surviving mechanism also preserves the work of instrument makers and woodworkers.

A surviving war turban combines a wicker frame, leather, quilted silk, velvet lining and muslin wrapping. Its steel face guard carries gold decoration and tiger forms. The National Army Museum traces this example from the spoils of 1799 through Cornwallis’s family, giving unusually clear evidence of its later journey.

At the Sèvres factory, Mysore’s ambassadors received a porcelain service made for Tipu and portrait busts as personal gifts. The busts were left unglazed, creating a marble-like surface. The surviving objects reveal diplomacy conducted through skilled manufacture as well as conversations and letters.

sections.title: Books, learning and a coin’s written voice

items.text: One Quran owned by Tipu had been copied in 1613, long before his reign. Persian tables were added for his use, including information about the chapters and their order of revelation. The book’s changing pages show an older manuscript being adapted for a later reader.

That manuscript’s leather binding has a triangular flap which tucks under the front cover to protect the page edges. It was stored flat. Gold-painted flowers decorate the margins. Protecting a valuable book could be a work of art in its own right.

In 1800, the naturalist Francis Buchanan recovered his own old botanical notebook. A colleague had accidentally taken it overseas; Mysore troops later captured it, and it was preserved and rebound in Tipu’s library. After the British conquest, Major Ogg returned it. This study notebook had travelled through a surprisingly eventful chain of owners.

Tipu issued coins in several metals and denominations through multiple mints. Henderson’s museum catalogue distinguishes large gold ahmadis from smaller pagodas and fanams, which fitted existing southern Indian currency traditions. New royal names and inscriptions therefore coexisted with familiar kinds of money.

A gold ahmadi dated 1198 in the Islamic calendar opens its reverse inscription with هو السلطان, huwa al-sulṭān, meaning “He is the Sultan.” The museum catalogue prints the Arabic and translates it. This short royal formula is authentic writing from Tipu’s coinage; it is Arabic, rather than a sample of everyday Kannada speech.

ending.text: The conquest of 1799 ended Tipu’s rule, but Mysore continued as a Wodeyar princely state under British supremacy. The map’s 1815 cutoff is not its fall. The kingdom survived into the twentieth century and became part of independent India in 1947; its communities and cultural traditions continued through these political changes.
